planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy crassula tolerates more shade than most succulents and spreads readily into a groundcover mat.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy crassula tolerates more shade than most succulents and spreads readily into a groundcover mat. Rounded, spotted, olive-green leaves cover a low, spreading succulent that tolerates considerably more shade than most crassula species, spreading by both creeping stems and tiny plantlets that form on airy flower stalks and drop to root nearby, quickly filling in as a low-maintenance groundcover under trees or along a shaded border edge. Its shade tolerance and easy, spreading habit make it a useful succulent groundcover option for the dry shade beneath established trees where few other succulents would survive. Water only occasionally, since it tolerates and even prefers drier shade conditions, and divide or thin the spreading mat as needed to control size.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Tom Thumb crassula is a compact selection well suited to a small pot or dish garden.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Tom Thumb crassula is a compact selection well suited to a small pot or dish garden. Tightly stacked, triangular, blue-green leaves alternate up trailing stems in a distinctive braided, chain-like pattern, blushing red-edged in bright light, on a more compact and slower-growing selection than the straight species that suits a smaller container or succulent dish garden. Its tidy, manageable size and interesting stacked-leaf texture make it a popular choice for succulent arrangements and windowsill collections where a naturally compact plant is preferred over more sprawling species. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best red edging, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Wine Cup crassula has an unusual funnel-shaped leaf and needs excellent drainage to avoid water pooling in the cupped foliage.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Wine Cup crassula has an unusual funnel-shaped leaf and needs excellent drainage to avoid water pooling in the cupped foliage. A single, oddly fused, funnel- or wine-cup-shaped leaf tops a short stem on this diminutive South African succulent, an extraordinary and instantly recognizable growth form unlike any other commonly grown crassula, with small white flowers rising from the center of the cup at maturity. Slow-growing and best displayed as a specimen where its unusual form can be appreciated up close, it is a favorite curiosity among succulent collectors for its bizarre, singular leaf shape. Water sparingly and carefully to avoid water pooling and rotting in the natural cup shape, provide bright indirect light, and propagate from leaf cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Copper Spoons develops its richest metallic bronze color in bright, direct light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Copper Spoons develops its richest metallic bronze color in bright, direct light. Thick, rounded, spoon-shaped leaves are coated in a dense, felted, rusty-copper fuzz on their new growth, aging to a more silvery-bronze tone, giving this Madagascar shrub a warm, metallic sheen unlike almost any other commonly grown succulent, produced on a substantial woody-based shrub that can eventually reach shoulder height or taller. Small yellow flowers appear occasionally but the plant is grown chiefly for its striking coppery foliage color, which intensifies with age and bright sun exposure. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide maximum bright light for the deepest copper coloring, and prune to shape as the shrub matures.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Velvet Leaf kalanchoe tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors best in bright conditions.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Velvet Leaf kalanchoe tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors best in bright conditions. Rounded, scalloped, gray-green leaves are covered in a soft, dense, velvety fuzz with faint bronze mottling along the margins, giving this Madagascar succulent a plush, tactile texture and subtle patterning quite different from the smoother, glossier leaves of most kalanchoe relatives. Its soft, fuzzy texture and manageable size make it a favorite for touch-friendly succulent displays where children or visitors can safely handle the plant without spines or sharp edges. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best coloring, and propagate easily from stem or leaf cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Bear's Paw needs excellent drainage and its fuzzy leaves are prone to rot if kept constantly wet or crowded.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Bear's Paw needs excellent drainage and its fuzzy leaves are prone to rot if kept constantly wet or crowded. Thick, plump, densely fuzzy green leaves are tipped with several small, reddish-brown, claw-like teeth along the leaf edge, an uncanny resemblance to a small bear's paw that gives this South African succulent its widely recognized common name and makes it an instant conversation piece in any succulent collection. Its distinctive, whimsical leaf shape and soft, velvety texture have made it one of the most popular novelty succulents sold, appealing to both collectors and casual houseplant buyers alike. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the fuzzy leaves to prevent spotting or rot, and provide bright light for compact growth.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Calico Hearts is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Calico Hearts is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering. Plump, rounded, heart-shaped leaves in olive-green are speckled with irregular reddish-brown or purple blotches, a distinctive mottled, calico-like pattern that gives this small South African succulent its common name and makes it a favorite for collectors seeking unusual leaf patterning on a manageable, windowsill-friendly scale. Slow-growing and clump-forming over time, it offsets gradually from the base and is easily propagated from individual leaves that root readily when allowed to callus before placing on soil. Water sparingly and only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and propagate from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Silver Bract pachyphytum holds its powdery silver coating best when kept dry and undisturbed.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Silver Bract pachyphytum holds its powdery silver coating best when kept dry and undisturbed. Thick, plump, oval leaves coated in a heavy, chalky, silvery-white powder are stacked densely at the tips of thick, upright-then-trailing stems, one of the more substantial pachyphytum species with larger leaves than the related and often-confused moonstones cultivars, producing red-and-white bell-shaped flowers on tall stalks in season. Native to rocky slopes in Mexico, it is easy to grow and propagate, though the delicate powdery coating rubs off easily with handling and should be protected to preserve the plant's silvery appearance. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid touching or wetting the leaves to protect the powdery bloom, and propagate from stem or leaf cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
